activities.caption: pair each consequence with its fact
activities.name: abFormationMatch

config.prompt: The astrobiological consequences of planet formation:

pairs.right: the Murchison meteorite (1969) carried amino acids formed in interstellar space
a Jupiter-sized outer guardian reduces impact rates — with a survivorship-bias caveat
may sterilise or eject the inner terrestrials

pairs.left: the timing on Earth was early
pairs.right: liquid water within a few hundred million years; chemical signatures by ~3.8 billion years ago

config.why: Life started early, which weakly suggests it is easy, given the real estate — but the claim rests on one system we can inspect closely.

activities.anchor: billions of candidate worlds in this galaxy alone
activities.caption: fill the blanks — reading a world from a dip
activities.name: abTransitCloze

config.text: Earth across the Sun dims it by (1/109)² ≈ 0.008% — about %%0%% parts per million — which is why %%1%% and %%2%% stare at hundreds of thousands of stars. JWST has now measured CO₂, SO₂ and %%3%% vapour in exoplanet atmospheres (WASP-39b, 2022).
config.hint: Two survey missions, one molecule you drink.

activities.caption: bet first — why M-dwarfs dominate despite the hazards
activities.name: abMDwarfPredict

config.q: Why do small, cool M-dwarfs dominate the search programmes, despite their flares and tidal locking?
choices: Transits are deeper, periods short, systems close enough for atmospheric spectroscopy — volume-efficient targets
Their flares help life evolve faster
They have no habitable zones, so the results are conclusive either way
config.why: TRAPPIST-1 is the archetype — and its JWST-era atmosphere results so far lean toward airless or thin: 'Earth-size in the zone' and 'habitable' remain different claims.

activities.anchor: impact history and time decide it
activities.caption: file the worlds — the zone is not the verdict
activities.name: abWorldBuckets

config.prompt: The zone is necessary, nowhere near sufficient. File each world:

items.label: Venus — inside the Sun's zone, a 460 °C pressure cooker
the Moon — in the zone, neither atmosphere nor water
Mars — at the zone's edge, its water gone
Europa — a subsurface ocean perhaps twice Earth's liquid water
Enceladus — plumes carrying water vapour, salts, organics and molecular hydrogen
Titan — methane lakes and a hydrological cycle in reverse solvent

config.why: The zone is only the band where liquid water can persist on a rocky surface given suitable atmosphere — Europa and Enceladus sit far outside any zone and likely hold oceans.

activities.anchor: a wet early surface, and a shallow subsurface where any surviving relic might persist
activities.caption: rebuild the redirect — from sunlight to chemistry
activities.name: abRedirectOrder

config.prompt: 1977 changed the search. Put the redirect in order:
items: Hydrothermal-vent ecosystems discovered — whole food webs on chemical energy, no sunlight
The toolkit redefined: water, carbon chemistry and a redox gradient
NASA's working definition: a self-sustaining chemical system capable of Darwinian evolution
The search points at the ocean moons — Europa, Enceladus, Titan
config.why: Earth's extremophiles redrew 'habitable' from the inside out — thermophiles above 100 °C, Deinococcus radiodurans shrugging off hospital-sterilising radiation.

activities.caption: call the magnitude — SETI's coverage so far
activities.name: abSetiEstimate

config.prompt: From Project Ozma (1960) to Breakthrough Listen today, how many stars have been surveyed without a confirmed artificial signal?
config.why: Over a million stars surveyed — plus optical laser-pulse searches and technosignature catalogues.
config.context: The first three Drake factors are now measured; life and intelligence have exactly one data point each.

activities.anchor: the equation tells you what to measure
activities.caption: find the faulty line — reasoning with N = 1
activities.name: abDrakeSpot

config.prompt: One line of this Drake-equation answer is wrong — click it:
lines: The Drake equation multiplies seven factors: star formation, planets, habitability, life, intelligence, communication, longevity.
The first three are now measured; life and intelligence have exactly one data point each.
The last factor — civilisation lifetime L — is precisely known from the archaeological record.
The equation's value is a research agenda: each factor names a measurable question.
config.correction: L is unknowable from a sample of one — and it dominates: a galaxy of long-lived civilisations gives a different sky from one where L is a few centuries.
config.why: The Fermi paradox's answers are all currently unfalsifiable speculation — the honest position is that the measurements have only begun.
